Taking the square root gives

$$

questions.problem: A triangle has sides $a$, $b$, and $c.$ The sides $a$, $b$, and $c$ are of lengths  $9$, $12$, and $18$, respectively. What is the measure of the angle between the sides $b$ and $c?$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/dede0326d992509dedf1c3a2854b47076ccc48ebf0e07705c8c12762d8ecdead.png)

We use the Law of Cosines to solve for angle $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2}}{2bc}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we have

$$
a=9,\,b=12,\,c=18.
$$

This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{12}^{2}+{18}^{2}-{9}^{2}}{2(12)(18)} \\  & =\frac{144+324-81}{432} \\  & =\frac{387}{432}\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠F & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{387}{432}) \\  & ={26.38}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have a general triangle where

- side $a$ is *opposite* angle $\angle A,$

- side $b$ is *opposite* angle $\angle B,$ and

- side $c$ is *opposite* angle $\angle C,$

as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

The **law of cosines** states that

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\ {b}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2ac\operatorname{cos}⁡B \\ {c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-2ab\operatorname{cos}⁡C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use this to calculate the length of one side when we know two sides and one angle.

If we look at the law of cosines we see that it's quite similar to the Pythagorean theorem:

$$
a^2+b^2=c^2
$$

But remember that the Pythagorean theorem can *only* be used for a *right-angled triangle*!

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/db9ed4aac9ca46ffc95d393d863cb09e9ba874caf0008410937f961fdf6c7ab6.png)

The law of cosines is more general and can be used on *any* triangle.

**Note:** To remember the law of cosines, it's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\begin{aligned}\,\text{side opposite}\, \\ \,\text{the angle}\,\end{aligned})}^{2}\,=\,{(\begin{aligned}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{side}\,\end{aligned})}^{2}\,+\,{(\begin{aligned}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{other side}\,\end{aligned})}^{2}\,-\,2(\begin{aligned}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{side}\,\end{aligned})(\begin{aligned}\,\text{adjacent}\, \\ \,\text{other side}\,\end{aligned})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\text{angle}).\end{aligned}
$$

We'll show how this formula can be derived at the end of the lesson.

tutorials.name: Using the Law of Cosines to Calculate an Unknown Angle
tutorials.problem:
Let's look at our general triangle again.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/8f3d3bf4824508ef152e8d8d567672d7d61fb36e0ffb533d97be7294e9198956.png)

When we know the lengths of three sides of a triangle, we rearrange the law of cosines to find an angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\ 2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A & ={b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2}}{2bc}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for all the angles, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡A & =\frac{{b}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{a}^{2}}{2bc}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡B & =\frac{{a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-{b}^{2}}{2ac}, \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡C & =\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-{c}^{2}}{2ab}.\end{aligned}
$$

It's helpful to notice that the equations always follow the same pattern:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\text{angle})=\frac{{(\begin{aligned}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{side}\end{aligned})}^{2}+{(\begin{aligned}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{other side}\end{aligned})}^{2}-{(\begin{aligned}\text{side opposite} \\ \text{the angle}\end{aligned})}^{2}}{2(\begin{aligned}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{side}\end{aligned})(\begin{aligned}\text{adjacent} \\ \text{other side}\end{aligned})}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Deriving the Law of Cosines
tutorials.problem:
Let's now derive the law of cosines in the following form:

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/7cc2a0cbb6a02af829e070fc54cfdbe616683f86527b119a530053a34048e699.png)

Let's now add the height $\overline{CH}$ and assume it has length $h,$ as shown.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14249653/assets/d4e80b2b54283ea353b687d959e9d8fc6c9303e85081c0a46b48703ee3dae7d5.png)

The remainder of this proof consists of two steps:

- **Step 1**: Write down expressions for $\cos A$ and $\sin A.$

- **Step 2**: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC,$ and simplify.

Using elementary trigonometry, we have

$$
\cos A = \dfrac{AH}{b}, \qquad \sin A = \dfrac{h}{b},
$$

which can be written as

$$
AH =  b\cos A, \qquad h = b\sin A.
$$

Applying the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle BHC$ and using our expression for $h,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{h}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, consider the length of the side $\overline{AB}.$ Since $\overline{AB}$ consists of two segments, $\overline{AH}$ and $\overline{BH},$ we have

$$
c = AH + BH\quad \Longrightarrow\quad BH = c - AH,
$$

and using our expression for $AH,$ we have

$$
BH = c - b\cos A.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $a^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2} & =(BH)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & =(c-b\operatorname{cos}⁡A)^{2}+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A+{b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡A+{b}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡A+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A \\  & ={b}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡A+{sin}^{2}⁡A)+{c}^{2}-2bc\operatorname{cos}⁡A.\end{aligned}
$$

It can be shown that $\cos^2A + \sin^2 A = 1$ for any angle $A$ (this is the Pythagorean theorem in trigonometric form). Therefore, we have

$$
a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A
$$

as required.

We can use a similar argument to prove the following results:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}^{2}={a}^{2}+{c}^{2}-2ac\operatorname{cos}⁡B \\ {c}^{2}={a}^{2}+{b}^{2}-2ab\operatorname{cos}⁡C\end{aligned}
$$
